title: Giving without a receipt
hook: give, and let it go; don't keep score

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanda's lamp: one small flame, lit with a whole heart, still burning at dawn. Your line was small and wholehearted.

There's a ledger that's easy to keep and hard to admit to. I drove last time. I paid for dinner twice. I remembered her birthday; she forgot mine. It's not greed exactly. It's bookkeeping. And the ledger turns gifts into loans: you gave, but somewhere in the back office, it was written down, with a due date. The giving week ends with the hardest part, the one that decides whether a gift stays a gift: what happens after you let go.
screen: `I DROVE LAST TIME.` → `THE LEDGER IN THE BACK OFFICE.` → `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER YOU LET GO.`

segments.voice: In one discourse, Sariputta asks the Buddha why the same gift can bear great fruit for one person and little for another. The Buddha answers with a ladder of motives. Someone gives hoping to get something back, thinking I'll enjoy the reward of this later. That's a gift, and it bears some fruit. Higher up, someone gives simply because giving is good, or because it's the family custom, or to follow the example of wise people of old, or because it makes the mind clear and glad. And at the top, someone gives as an ornament and a support for the mind. Same rice, same bowl. What changes is what the giver is holding onto. A later Mahayana text, the Diamond Sutra, pushes further: a bodhisattva should give without dwelling on anything, not on sights, not on sounds, not on anything the mind could grab. Later teachers put it as three things held lightly: the giver, the gift, the receiver. Give like a hand that opens and doesn't close again to check what it gave; teachers sometimes call it giving that leaves no trace. The Pali word for that kind of generosity is caga, which also means letting go, relinquishing. Generosity and letting go are the same word. The week so far: giving first opens the door. The bowl is open. Glad before, bright during, happy after. Share the last bite. Attention is a gift. Small and wholehearted. And the last step: no receipt. Nobody's saying you can't notice who never pays; you can still be wise. But the gift itself, once it leaves your hand, is finished. It doesn't need a signature.
screen: `A LADDER OF MOTIVES.` · `AT THE TOP: AN ORNAMENT FOR THE MIND.` · `GIVE WITHOUT DWELLING ON ANYTHING.` · `CAGA: GENEROSITY IS LETTING GO.` · then, large: `NO RECEIPT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one gift you're still keeping track of, a favor that wasn't returned or a kindness nobody noticed, written as a line in the ledger, dated. With the out-breath, imagine tearing up the receipt, not because they deserved it, but because the gift was already complete. Breathe out again, let the hand open, and rest in whatever lightness comes.
Caga. Generosity, letting go: giving without a receipt, no score kept, the gift complete the moment it leaves your hand.
Your line: no receipt. Generosity and letting go are one word. The giving week ends here.

howItsDone: Some Buddhists give anonymously or without expecting return, and in Mahayana traditions the perfection of giving is described as giving without clinging to the gift, the receiver or the self as giver.

notes: The ladder of motives is condensed from AN 7.49 (it has seven steps, including 'I cook, they don't; it's not right not to give' and 'my good name will spread' in some readings); confirm the paraphrase.
The Diamond Sutra passage (section 4) is paraphrased; 'giving that leaves no trace' is a teaching phrase, not a quotation.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer claims 'most of us' keep a ledger; the AN 7.49 ladder now keeps 'clear and glad' and 'ornament for the mind' as separate steps (the script had merged them); the Diamond Sutra section 4 paraphrase now says what the text says (not dwelling on sights, sounds and so on), and the giver-gift-receiver triad is credited to later teachers; the practice no longer repeats day 134's body-tightness check.
